• AR Rahman's agent warned him against taking Slumdog Millionaire in 2008: "Don't do this because you might get fired" — Danny Boyle, the rep said, "works with multiple people... He might throw your score out very soon. It happened to some of our clients."
  • Rahman ignored the advice, composed the score in secret over three weeks across New York, Mumbai and Chennai — even his own team thought it was a documentary — with Boyle visiting every evening for notes.
  • He stepped away from Ashutosh Gowariker's What's Your Rashee (starring Priyanka Chopra) to make the time. The film used only 17–18 music cues, against ~150 for a normal film.
  • The payoff: two Oscars at the 2009 Academy Awards (Best Original Score and Best Original Song for "Jai Ho"), plus two Grammys, a Golden Globe and a BAFTA.

Before "Jai Ho" became a global anthem, the project nearly never happened — because AR Rahman's own people told him to walk away. In a recent recollection reported by The Indian Express, Rahman revealed that his agent warned him not to take Slumdog Millionaire in 2008, cautioning that director Danny Boyle might discard his work.

"Don't do this because you might get fired," the agent told him. Boyle, the representative warned, "works with multiple people... He might throw your score out very soon. It happened to some of our clients. It's controversial."

Trusting his instinct

Rahman had seen the film and felt otherwise. "Okay, nobody will know that I got fired if I don't tell it out. So, I scored the movie and Danny was amazing," he said. "Sometimes, people confuse you but you have to think what you have to do, what is right."

"I did it in secret. The team thought it was a documentary or something like that."

— AR Rahman

Three weeks, three cities

What followed was one of the most compressed scoring schedules of his career: three weeks, split between New York, Mumbai and Chennai, with mixing in London. Boyle visited him every evening for notes. Rahman later noted the film's unusual economy with music — "Boyle uses music very less but very efficiently" — with only 17–18 cues against the roughly 150 a normal film would carry.

To make the time, he stepped away from Ashutosh Gowariker's What's Your Rashee, starring Priyanka Chopra. Boyle had approached Rahman after hearing his music in Rang De Basanti, and the collaboration quickly warmed: Rahman has described Boyle as "like a friend... it was like working for Mani Ratnam."

The payoff

The gamble paid off beyond anyone's imagining. At the 2009 Academy Awards, Rahman won two Oscars — Best Original Score and Best Original Song for "Jai Ho" — followed by two Grammy Awards, a Golden Globe and a BAFTA. "Jai Ho" itself was written for the end credits after Rahman felt the film's closing needed an original number, replacing a placeholder track in the shot footage.

Seventeen years on, the anecdote — first told in a 2025 interview at the Toronto International Film Festival and resurfaced this week — remains the definitive case study in backing your instincts over risk-averse counsel. The agent's warning is now a footnote; the score is history.
diaspora_angle: An iconic Indian-artist-on-world-stage story — the diaspora takes pride in Rahman's Oscars and the 'Jai Ho' cultural moment, and the trust-your-instincts arc is strong human interest.
headline: AR Rahman Was Told Not to Work With Danny Boyle — He Won Two Oscars Instead
subheadline: Warned that Danny Boyle might throw out his score, Rahman composed the Slumdog Millionaire music in secret over three weeks — and collected two Oscars, two Grammys, a Golden Globe and a BAFTA.
